prelims.text: Extradition Act, 1962 is the legislative basis for extradition from India, which also needs a treaty, agreement or arrangement.
India-US Extradition Treaty was signed on 25 June 1997 and entered into force on 21 July 1999.
India is party to the Hague Service Convention and objects to Article 10 service by postal channels.
US Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, 1976: foreign states are immune from US courts except as provided in sections 1605 to 1607.
MEA is India's Central Authority for extradition requests; Letters Rogatory and MLAT requests are separate channels for legal assistance.

mains.text: India-US treaty bars extradition for political offences (Article 4) and does not allow nationality as a ground for refusal (Article 3).
FSIA exceptions to immunity include waiver, commercial activity in the US and tortious acts causing harm in the US.
Halkbank (US Supreme Court): FSIA gives no immunity from criminal prosecution, so civil and criminal immunity routes differ.
Extradition Act, 1962 places no bar on extraditing Indian nationals, so India's own practice cuts both ways.
Contest jurisdiction on sovereign-immunity grounds and route evidence requests through treaty-based legal assistance rather than public confrontation.

prelims.text: Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) lists ten tribal areas: Assam 3, Meghalaya 3, Tripura 1, Mizoram 3, each an autonomous district.
A Sixth Schedule District Council has at most 30 members: up to four nominated by the Governor, the rest elected on adult suffrage.
The Bardoloi Committee drafted the Sixth Schedule to protect tribal areas and customs while enabling their development.
Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Act, 1997 (Act XXXI of 1997) provides for hill councils and an Inter-District Advisory Council.
Leh's hill council began in 1995 on the Darjeeling pattern; Kargil's followed in July 2003.

mains.text: Sixth Schedule councils may levy land revenue and taxes and regulate money-lending and trading by non-tribals.
Ramachandran Committee recommended stating the minimum powers of District Councils in the Constitution, since devolved powers differ.
125th Amendment Bill, 2019 proposed larger councils, village and municipal councils and wider law-making powers for Sixth Schedule councils.
Autonomy is conditional: council regulations need the Governor's approval, and the Governor may assume council functions if administration fails.
Legislate minimum devolved powers and village and municipal tiers, as the 125th Amendment Bill proposed.

prelims.text: CPCB is a statutory body under the Water Act, 1974 with powers and functions under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981.
National AQI has six categories (Good to Severe) built from eight pollutants; the worst sub-index decides the AQI.
NCAP (January 2019) covers 131 cities; target is up to 40% PM10 reduction or the 60 microgram per cubic metre standard by 2025-26.
A non-attainment city exceeds NAAQS for five consecutive years and has at least three monitoring stations.
GRAP was notified in January 2017 on CPCB's recommendation; CAQM, constituted in 2021, now publishes the revised GRAP.

mains.text: Air Act, 1981 section 16: CPCB advises the Centre and plans a nation-wide programme for prevention, control and abatement of air pollution.
NCAP: 95 of 131 cities improved annual PM10 in 2023-24 against 2017-18, and 18 met the PM10 standard.
NCAP earmarked Rs 19,614.44 crore for 131 cities (2019-20 to 2025-26): 49 via the XV Finance Commission grant, 82 via MoEFCC.
Implementation lags: by December 2023, Rs 9,650 crore was released to NCAP cities but about Rs 5,835 crore utilised.
Track city action plans on the PRANA portal and keep grants performance-based on measured PM10 reductions.

prelims.text: National Waterways Act, 2016 declared 111 inland waterways (including 5 earlier ones) as National Waterways across 24 states.
National Waterway 110 is the Yamuna: 1,080 km across Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.
NW-1 is the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly system from Haldia to Allahabad (1,620 km), the longest of the five original waterways.
Inland Waterways Authority of India was constituted in 1985 to augment waterway transport capacity.
Jal Marg Vikas Project on NW-1 (Haldia to Varanasi) is World Bank-assisted and costs Rs 5,369.18 crore.

mains.text: National Waterways Act, 2016 provides for declaring inland waterways as national waterways and regulating and developing them for shipping and navigation.
JMVP fairway works target least available depth of 3.0 m (Haldia-Barh), 2.5 m (Barh-Ghazipur) and 2.2 m (Ghazipur-Varanasi).
Operational national waterways carried about 72.31 million tonnes per annum of cargo (March 2020).
Viability is limited: only 26 of 111 waterways passed techno-economic feasibility for cargo or passenger movement, so cruises will not scale everywhere.
Maintain least available depth through fairway works and match vessel draught to river depth, as JMVP does on NW-1.

prelims.text: Article 324(1): Election Commission superintends, directs and controls electoral rolls and elections to Parliament, State legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
RP Act, 1950 section 21: rolls are prepared by a qualifying date and revised before general elections and bye-elections.
Each State has a Chief Electoral Officer (RP Act, 1950 section 13A) who supervises preparation, revision and correction of rolls.
Article 324(2): the Election Commission comprises the Chief Election Commissioner and other Commissioners the President fixes, appointed subject to parliamentary law.
Article 327 lets Parliament legislate on elections, expressly subject to the Constitution, including Article 324.

mains.text: Section 21(3) RP Act, 1950 lets the Commission, for recorded reasons, order a special revision of any constituency or part of it.
Supreme Court: Article 324 operates in areas left unoccupied by legislation; its words are of the broadest amplitude.
2026 INSC 564 (SIR): Articles 324 and 327 are complementary, and section 21(3) RP Act supplies statutory authority for special revision.
Plenary power is not unbounded: the Commission cannot defy an express statutory prohibition, so deletions must stay within RP Act rules.
Strengthen CEO and DEO supervision and record reasons for revisions; the existing roll stays in force until a special revision finishes.

prelims.text: PLFS was launched by NSO in April 2017; LFPR is the share of the labour force in the population, WPR the employed share.
From 2025 the PLFS survey period moved from July-June to the January-December calendar year.
Usual status (ps+ss) classifies activity over the preceding 365 days, combining principal and subsidiary status.
Current Weekly Status classifies a person as employed if working at least one hour in the preceding seven days.
PLFS 2025 (usual status, 15+): female LFPR 40.0% against male 79.1%; female WPR 38.8%.

mains.text: Female WPR (usual status, 15+) rose from 22.0% in 2017-18 to 40.3% in 2023-24.
Agriculture's employment share eased only from 44.8% (2024) to 43.0% (2025) and it remains the largest employer.
In 2019-20, 60% of women workers were in agriculture, 17% in industry and 23% in services.
Women's regular wage or salaried share rose from 16.6% (2024) to 18.2% (2025).
Expand women's regular and manufacturing jobs; PLFS 2025 shows manufacturing's worker share rising as agriculture's falls.

prelims.text: Indra Sawhney v Union of India (16 November 1992) upheld 27% OBC reservation under Article 16(4), set a 50% ceiling and mandated creamy-layer exclusion.
DoPT OM of 8 September 1993 gave 27% reservation in central civil posts and excluded the creamy layer through six categories.
Mandal Commission was the second Backward Classes Commission, appointed under Article 340 (31 December 1979).
Creamy-layer income limit: Rs 1 lakh (1993), Rs 2.5 lakh (2004), then Rs 4.5 lakh by later revision.
EWS 10% quota rests on Articles 15(6) and 16(6) (103rd Amendment, 2019) and sits outside the 50% limit of Articles 15(4) and 16(4).

mains.text: Indra Sawhney: non-exclusion of the creamy layer would violate Articles 14 and 16, so exclusion is a constitutional necessity.
Indra Sawhney directed criteria within four months; the Expert Committee centred them on social status, not income alone.
NCBC supplementary report advised raising the creamy-layer limit from Rs 6 lakh to Rs 15 lakh, noting 27% OBC vacancies stayed unfilled.
OBC share in direct recruitment to central civil posts reached 34.52% in 2018 against the 27% quota.
Sawhney held exclusion should not be merely economic; stringent income limits left quota posts unfilled.
Revise the limit periodically and keep exclusion rooted in social advancement, as Indra Sawhney and NCBC advised.

prelims.text: Outer Space Treaty, 1967 Article II: outer space is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, use or occupation.
Outer Space Treaty Article VI: States bear responsibility for national space activities, including private entities that need authorisation and continuing supervision.
Outer Space Treaty Article VIII: the State of registry retains jurisdiction and control over a launched object and its personnel.
Telecommunications Act, 2023 section 4: Centre owns spectrum for the people; assignment is by auction except First Schedule entries, assigned administratively.
DoT has issued GMPCS, NLD and ISP Category A authorisations for NGSO satellite services; spectrum terms were referred to TRAI.

mains.text: Section 4 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 makes auction the default and administrative assignment the exception for First Schedule entries.
Outer Space Treaty Article VI makes the home State supervise private operators, a template for authorising foreign constellations.
Industry (ISpA) argues satellite spectrum is shared and non-exclusive worldwide, and that auctions risk reciprocal action against Indian operators.
Finalise TRAI's 2026 Satellite Communication Network authorisation framework under section 3(1)(b), which stakeholders link to Indian incorporation and IN-SPACe authorisation.

prelims.text: CARICOM Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice (endorsed March 2014) seeks apology, repatriation, cultural institutions and debt cancellation.
Durban Declaration (2001): slavery and the slave trade are a crime against humanity and should always have been so.
Caribbean Court of Justice was inaugurated at Port of Spain on 16 April 2005 with original jurisdiction under the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas.
CCJ appellate cases come from Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Guyana and Saint Lucia.
Jamaica signed the CCJ Agreement in 2001 but does not send final appeals to the CCJ.

mains.text: Durban Declaration paragraph 34 notes some States apologised and paid reparation where appropriate for grave violations.
An estimated 25 to 30 million people were forcibly uprooted from Africa through enslavement and the slave trade.
UN experts recommend States consider CARICOM's ten-point plan as a guiding framework for reparatory justice.
Legal controversies persist, such as the intertemporal principle, though speakers argue crimes against humanity carry no limitation period.
CERD General Recommendation 40 asks States for time-bound national action plans combining monetary, non-monetary and structural reparatory measures.

prelims.text: IndiaAI Mission has an outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years (approved March 2024), run by IndiaAI under MeitY.
IndiaAI Mission has seven pillars; the compute pillar is the largest, with nearly 45% of funding.
India's installed data-centre capacity grew from 375 MW (2020) to about 1,575 MW.
MeghRaj (GI Cloud) was set up under Digital India to meet the Government of India's cloud needs.
DPDP Act, 2023 section 16 lets the Centre restrict transfer of personal data to notified countries.

mains.text: IndiaAI Mission has onboarded over 38,000 GPUs at Rs 65 per hour, about one-third of the global average, plus 1,050 TPUs.
Cloud data-centre capacity of about 1,280 MW is expected to grow four to five times by 2030.
DPDP Rules: Significant Data Fiduciaries must follow government directions on restricted data categories, including localisation where required.
DPDP allows transfers abroad except to notified countries, without assessing foreign data-protection adequacy, a gap PRS flagged.
Spread data-centre hubs beyond metros, as Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal emerge, while enforcing localisation norms.

prelims.text: HDI has three dimensions: life expectancy at birth, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita.
HDI aggregates the three dimension indices by geometric mean and uses the logarithm of income.
HDI goalposts: life expectancy 20-85 years, expected schooling 0-18, mean schooling 0-15, GNI per capita $100-75,000 (2021 PPP).
India's HDI was 0.685 in 2023, rank 130 of 193, in the medium category (high starts at 0.700).
NITI Aayog's MPI 2023: Kerala has the lowest multidimensional poverty among States, at 0.002.

mains.text: Kerala's life expectancy is 75 years against 70 nationally, maternal mortality 19 against 97, and infant mortality is single-digit.
Kerala topped the SDG India Index 2023-24 for the fourth consecutive year, scoring 79.
Kerala's four missions: Aardram (health), LIFE (housing), Public Education Rejuvenation and Haritha Keralam.
NITI's health index ranked Kerala first overall but last (21st of 21 larger States) in incremental progress, as early gains plateau.
Plan for ageing: Kerala's 60+ share was 11.8% (2011) and is expected above 20%, raising chronic-disease demand.

prelims.text: DoPT OM of 8 September 1993 fixed creamy-layer criteria; income from salaries or agricultural land is not clubbed under the income/wealth test.
Creamy-layer income limit is ₹8 lakh a year, raised from ₹6 lakh, effective 1 September 2017.
Indra Sawhney (1992), a nine-judge bench, upheld 27% OBC reservation under Article 16(4), capped total reservation ordinarily at 50% and mandated creamy-layer exclusion.
Article 340 empowers the President to appoint a commission to investigate conditions of socially and educationally backward classes.
Article 16(4) permits reservation in State posts for any backward class not adequately represented in State services.

mains.text: M. Nagaraj (2006): the 50% ceiling, creamy layer and compelling reasons are constitutional requirements without which Article 16 equality would collapse.
The Ram Nandan Prasad Expert Committee, accepted in toto, centred creamy-layer criteria on social status of positions rather than income alone.
Article 16(4) enables reservation for backward classes, but the Constitution is silent on creamy layer, a judicial doctrine from Indra Sawhney.
NCBC's 2015 supplementary report noted OBCs had filled not more than 16% of the 27% quota.
A parliamentary committee felt creamy layer indirectly brings in the economic criteria the constitutional framers rejected.
forward] Settle equivalence of PSU and private posts with government posts and revise the income criterion every three years, as the 1993 OM envisaged.

prelims.text: Article 31B protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule from challenge as violating fundamental rights; the 76th Amendment (1994) added Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation Act.
Indra Sawhney (16 November 1992) held total reservations under Article 16(4) should not exceed 50%.
Article 16(4B), inserted by the 81st Amendment (2000), keeps carried-forward unfilled vacancies outside the 50% ceiling of the year they are filled.
Articles 15(6) and 16(6), inserted by the 103rd Amendment (2019), give EWS 10% reservation outside the 50% limit on Articles 15(4) and 16(4).
Maratha reservation case (5 May 2021): the Supreme Court held the 50% limit crossable only in extraordinary circumstances backed by quantifiable, contemporaneous data.

mains.text: Indra Sawhney (1992) fixed the 50% ceiling; the Maratha ruling (2021) refused to exceed it without extraordinary circumstances and data.
Article 16(4) permits reservation for inadequately represented backward classes; Article 15(4) permits special provisions for SCs, STs and backward classes.
Tamil Nadu's 69% Act of 1994 was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 76th Amendment to secure protection under Article 31B.
Karnataka Act 1 of 2023 recites that the Government was satisfied of extraordinary circumstances to raise SC and ST quotas above 15% and 3%.
The Union told Parliament in 2021 it has no proposal to override the Indra Sawhney 50% limit, narrowing political routes to higher quotas.
forward] Gather quantifiable, contemporaneous data on backwardness and representation to justify any breach, as the Maratha reservation ruling requires.

prelims.text: MDR is a fee merchants pay payment processors on card or UPI transactions, typically a percentage of transaction value.
From January 2020, zero MDR on RuPay debit and BHIM-UPI came through Section 10A of the PSS Act, 2007 and Section 269SU, Income-tax Act.
NPCI clarified MDR of 0.4% on UPI P2M transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above.
All person-to-person UPI transactions stay free; small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh a month through QR keep zero MDR.
Cabinet's FY 2024-25 incentive scheme pays 0.15% on UPI P2M transactions up to ₹2,000 for small merchants.

mains.text: The August 2026 PSS Act amendment lets the Centre notify payment modes on which no charge can be levied; UPI up to ₹2,000 is notified.
A ₹1,500 crore incentive scheme (FY 2024-25) supports low-value BHIM-UPI P2M transactions and compensates acquiring banks.
MDR will apply to about 4% of merchant transactions; 5% of MDR collections will fund small-merchant UPI adoption.
Government says MDR is not a tax and customers do not pay it, yet banks must stop merchants passing it on.
forward] Keep thin-margin sectors on the flat ₹5 charge and ring-fence the small-merchant fund so zero-MDR coverage and adoption continue.

prelims.text: 97th Amendment inserted Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT) and Article 43B, and made forming cooperatives a fundamental right under Article 19.
Article 243ZJ: a board has at most 21 directors and a five-year term; co-opted members have no vote.
Article 243ZL: no board may be superseded or suspended beyond six months; one year for non-multi-State banking cooperatives.
Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021): Part IXB held operative only for multi-State societies and Union territories, not State societies.
Ministry of Cooperation is the nodal Centre ministry; Article 243ZR applies Part IXB to multi-State societies, reading State as Centre.

mains.text: Rajendra N. Shah (2021): 'co-operative societies' is State List Entry 32, and Part IXB lacked ratification by half the States for State societies.
Article 243ZI lets State legislatures regulate cooperatives on voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation and autonomous functioning.
Article 243ZJ denies co-opted members a vote, so voting nominees sit uneasily with democratic member-control.
The Joint Committee on the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Bill 2022 aligned the Act with the 97th Amendment, including SC/ST and women board seats.
forward] Align State laws with Part IXB: elections by an independent authority, fixed terms and limited supersession.

prelims.text: Section 69A, IT Act 2000 lets the Centre direct blocking of information in the interest of sovereignty, defence, State security, foreign relations or public order.
Blocking Rules 2009 (27 October 2009): a Designated Officer not below Joint Secretary issues directions after a committee examines the request.
Shreya Singhal (24 March 2015) held Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules constitutionally valid, calling it narrowly drawn with safeguards.
Sahyog portal, run by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), sends takedown notices to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b).
I4C has blocked over 2,77,053 illegal apps, websites, accounts and links through Sahyog and proactive intimation to intermediaries.

mains.text: Under the 69A Rules, the IT Secretary blocks on a Joint Secretary-level committee's recommendation, and the originator gets a hearing.
Shreya Singhal (2015): intermediaries disable content only on a court or government order; Section 69A survived as narrowly drawn.
I4C has blocked over 2,77,053 illegal apps, websites, accounts and links through Sahyog and proactive action.
Sahyog notices rest on Section 79(3)(b), a separate route from Section 69A's committee-reviewed blocking orders.
forward] Publish blocking and takedown data and ensure originators get a hearing, as the 69A Rules provide, to meet Shreya Singhal safeguards.

prelims.text: CGFMU was set up in January 2016 under National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC), a wholly owned Government of India company.
PMMY, launched 8 April 2015, gives collateral-free loans to non-farm micro enterprises through banks, NBFCs and MFIs.
PMMY categories: Shishu up to ₹50,000; Kishor to ₹5 lakh; Tarun to ₹10 lakh; Tarun Plus to ₹20 lakh.
Tarun Plus, effective 24 October 2024, is for entrepreneurs who repaid Tarun loans; CGFMU covers PMMY loans up to ₹20 lakh.
From FY 2020-21, SHG loans of ₹10–20 lakh also qualify for CGFMU cover.

mains.text: Under PMMY, ₹33.65 lakh crore was sanctioned by March 2025; Shishu was 78% of loans but 35% of the amount.
CGFMU guarantees PMMY loans by lending institutions, reducing credit risk and enabling collateral-free credit to micro enterprises.
A 2% interest subvention on Shishu loans for 12 months (FY 2020-21) eased borrower credit costs under Aatmanirbhar Bharat.
Larger loans remain thin: Tarun Plus was only 0.095% of the amount sanctioned.
forward] Use CGFMU cover to move borrowers up the Shishu, Kishor, Tarun and Tarun Plus ladder as businesses grow.

prelims.text: Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 (24 August 2022) cover EV, portable, automotive and industrial batteries on an EPR basis.
Producers must use a minimum share of domestically recycled materials in new batteries from FY 2027-28.
The rules prohibit landfilling and incineration of waste batteries; a centralised online EPR portal handles certificates.
National Critical Mineral Mission runs to 2030-31 with a ₹16,300 crore outlay, covering 24 critical minerals including lithium and cobalt.
Ministry of Mines' ₹1,500 crore scheme incentivises extracting critical minerals from e-waste and spent lithium-ion batteries.

mains.text: EPR makes producers responsible for collection, recycling and refurbishment; environmental compensation applies on shortfalls under the polluter pays principle.
Producers procured EPR certificates for 7.29 lakh tonnes of battery metals against a 10.96 lakh tonne target.
The ₹1,500 crore recycling scheme caps incentive at ₹50 crore for big and ₹25 crore for small recyclers.
Black-mass processing capacity is limited, so it was exported before extracting minerals; spent LIBs are about 60 kilotonnes a year.
Very few Indian players do end-to-end battery scrap to metal recycling, so an export ban can strain processing capacity.
forward] Incentivise mineral extraction rather than black-mass production and formalise collection under EPR to retain critical minerals.

prelims.text: Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum will occupy North and South Blocks under the Central Vista Redevelopment Project, New Delhi.
The Prime Minister first announced the museum at the International Museum Expo in May 2023.
India signed a technical cooperation agreement with France Museums Développement on 19 December 2024 for the museum.
The Government vacated North and South Blocks on 13 February 2026 for Seva Teerth and Kartavya Bhavans; the Cabinet made them museum space.
National Museum, established 1949 in New Delhi, houses around 2 lakh objects across 22 galleries; its current building opened in 1960.

mains.text: Ministry of Culture plans a museum showcasing over 10,000 years of civilisational journey through thematic, non-linear storytelling.
The France Museums Développement partnership covers a feasibility study, interpretive planning and building programming.
PIB describes the museum as spread over 1,54,000 sq m and billed as the world's largest museum.
Project timeline and budget were contingent on the feasibility study, leaving cost and heritage-conversion risks.
forward] Use digitisation under the Google Arts & Culture MoU to give early public access while galleries are built.

prelims.text: SBM-Urban launched 2 October 2014; SBM-U 2.0 launched 1 October 2021 for five years.
Swachh Survekshan, conducted by MoHUA since 2016, is the annual survey ranking cities on cleanliness.
SBM-U 2.0 targets: all statutory towns ODF+, towns under 1 lakh ODF++, half of them Water+, all 3-star Garbage Free.
Urban India was declared open defecation free in 2019; over 3,000 cities were ODF+ and over 950 ODF++ at SBM-U 2.0 launch.
By April 2023, 14 cities including Indore, Surat, Navi Mumbai and Vijayawada were certified Water+.

mains.text: SBM-U 2.0 aims at 100% source segregation, scientific waste management and remediation of all legacy dumpsites.
Of 4,910 ULBs, PIB records 4,314 ODF+, 1,973 ODF++ and 214 Water+.
The MoHUA Secretary cited Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu as exemplary States in solid-waste management.
The minister said all cities reaching 3-star Garbage Free status by 2026 needs accelerated efforts, signalling a gap between rankings and delivery.
forward] Stress source segregation, integration of the informal sector and operating EPRs to sustain gains beyond rankings.

prelims.text: Framework for an Interim Agreement announced 7 February 2026; broader US-India Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) talks were launched on 13 February 2025.
US to apply a reciprocal tariff of 18% on originating Indian goods including textiles, leather, plastics and organic chemicals.
India to eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and many food and agricultural products such as tree nuts and soybean oil.
India intends to purchase $500 billion of US energy, aircraft, precious metals, technology products and coking coal over five years.
India-US Trade Policy Forum was established in 2005; the 14th TPF met in New Delhi on 12 January 2024.
Rules of origin to ensure benefits accrue predominately to the US and India; both commit to preferential market access in sectors of respective interest.

mains.text: Framework commits both sides to address non-tariff barriers: US medical devices, restrictive ICT import licensing and acceptance of US or international standards within six months of entry into force.
Either country may modify its commitments if the other changes the agreed tariffs, building a reversibility clause into the framework.
Economic security alignment: supply chain resilience, inbound and outbound investment reviews, export controls and digital trade rules via the BTA.
India would buy $500 billion of US goods by 2031; US to remove reciprocal tariffs on pharmaceuticals and aircraft parts only if the interim deal concludes.
On 20 February 2026 the US Supreme Court held reciprocal tariffs illegal; the US re-imposed tariffs and India's Commerce Ministry said it was examining implications.
Use BTA negotiations to expand market access and press the US request to keep lowering tariffs on Indian goods, while protecting sensitive farm and dairy sectors.

prelims.text: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 was launched on 31 March 2023 and came into effect on 1 April 2023.
FTP 2023 targets $2 trillion of goods and services exports by 2030.
RoDTEP has been implemented since 1 January 2021; from 15 December 2022 it covers pharmaceuticals, chemicals and iron and steel articles.
RoSCTL has operated since 7 March 2019 to support labour-oriented textile exports.
District Export Promotion Committees are chaired by the Collector and co-chaired by the DGFT Regional Authority under Districts as Export Hubs.

mains.text: RoDTEP covers 10,642 tariff lines at 8-digit level; the FY 2025-26 budget allocation is ₹18,232.50 crore.
Districts as Export Hubs adopts a bottoms-up approach: identify export products in each district, address bottlenecks and generate local employment.
FTP 2023 prioritises SCOMET dual-use items, e-commerce exports and collaboration with States and Districts, and relies on process re-engineering and automation.
RoDTEP benefit of ₹42,036 crore was granted from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2024.
Raise FTA utilisation through the Common Digital Platform for Certificates of Origin and diversify markets through trade agreements.

prelims.text: Quad came together during the 2004 tsunami response; elevated to leaders' level in 2021, with the first virtual summit on 12 March 2021.
Formally the grouping is the 'Quad', not the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue; four pillars include maritime and transnational security and critical technologies.
Leaders' summits: Tokyo 24 May 2022, Hiroshima 20 May 2023, Wilmington 21 September 2024.
IPMDA was launched at the 2022 Tokyo summit to give partners near-real-time maritime domain data.
MAITRI, the Maritime Initiative for Training in the Indo-Pacific, was announced at Wilmington in 2024 with India hosting the first workshop.

mains.text: IPMDA helps over two dozen countries access dark-vessel data through the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency, Southeast Asia and IFC-IOR Gurugram.
Wilmington launched the Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, Quad Indo-Pacific Logistics Network pilot and Quad Ports of the Future Partnership.
Quad Infrastructure Fellowships expanded to over 2,200 experts, with well over 1,300 fellowships already provided.
Quad Cancer Moonshot, announced in 2024, targets cervical cancer in the Indo-Pacific using public and private resources.
Leaders committed to secure Quad funding through national budgets and deepen interparliamentary exchanges so the grouping endures beyond summitry.

prelims.text: Deep Ocean Mission was approved by the Cabinet in 2021 at ₹4,077 crore for five years, implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
Deep Ocean Mission was launched w.e.f. 7 September 2021 as a Central Sector Scheme; Samudrayaan is a project under it.
Matsya-6000 is built to operate for 12 hours normally and sustain up to 96 hours in emergencies.
A 2.1 m titanium alloy human sphere is being developed with the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre of ISRO.
Ocean Mineral Explorer OMe 6000, a deep-water AUV, has been deployed for exploration under the mission.

mains.text: Deep Ocean Mission has six components including deep-sea mining and submersible technology, ocean climate advisory services and an Advanced Marine Station for Ocean Biology.
Target resources are nickel, cobalt, rare earths and manganese, accessible only through direct human observation and sampling at depth.
India joins the USA, Russia, Japan, France and China as countries with manned subsea vehicles.
Wet harbour trials of the 500 m human submersible were completed and pilots trained aboard France's NAUTILE in 2025.
Commercial deep-sea mineral exploration should follow global rules set by the International Seabed Authority.

prelims.text: UAPA 1967 section 3(1): Centre may declare an association unlawful by notification in the Official Gazette.
Section 4: Centre must refer the notification to the UAPA Tribunal within thirty days; the Tribunal decides within six months.
Section 3(3): the notification has no effect until the Tribunal confirms it, except where immediate effect is directed for reasons stated in writing.
Section 6: a confirmed notification stays in force for five years from the date it becomes effective.
Section 13(1): taking part in or abetting unlawful activity is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

mains.text: Section 6(2) lets the Centre cancel a notification any time, on its own motion or on an aggrieved person's application, whether or not the Tribunal confirmed it.
Section 3(2) requires grounds in the notification but does not require disclosure of facts the Centre considers against public interest.
The Centre declared four Jammu and Kashmir Peoples League factions unlawful on 15 March 2024; the Tribunal confirmed on 29 August 2024.
Sections 7 and 8 empower the Centre to prohibit use of funds and notify places used by a banned association.
Where privilege is claimed the Tribunal itself examines the material without disclosing it to the association, limiting the association's ability to contest the grounds.
Ensure timely Tribunal adjudication within the six-month limit and reasoned review of renewals so bans stay proportionate.

prelims.text: FCRA 2010 replaced the 1976 Act; Presidential assent was on 26 September 2010.
2020 amendment: foreign contribution only in an 'FCRA account' at State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch; sub-granting to other associations prohibited.
2020 amendment cut the administrative expense ceiling from 50% to 20% of foreign contribution received.
Registration ceases after five years unless renewed; the 2020 amendment requires Aadhaar or passport details of office-bearers.
Suspension of registration is up to 180 days, extendable by a further 180 days after the 2020 amendment.

mains.text: Centre cancelled over 19,000 recipient registrations between 2011 and 2019, the Statement of Objects of the 2020 Bill recorded.
Section 3 bars foreign contribution to election candidates and others, and to acceptance that harms sovereignty, integrity, security or communal harmony.
Government says FCRA is a transparency and disclosure framework, not a ban: receipts must be registered, channelled through a designated account and reported.
Nearly 20,000 cancelled registrations and about 15,000 deemed ceased left thousands of crore of assets in limbo under Section 15 vesting.
Provide a clear State authority to take possession of assets of cancelled registrations and ensure proportionate, hearing-based cancellation.

prelims.text: SCO was established on 15 June 2001 by China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan; its predecessor Shanghai Five formed in April 1996.
India and Pakistan became full members on 9 June 2017 at the Astana Summit; India had observer status since July 2005.
Iran became a member at the SCO summit hosted virtually by India on 4 July 2023.
SCO now lists ten members including Belarus; India assumed the rotating chairmanship in 2023.
The 25th SCO Summit at Tianjin approved the SCO Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats and an SCO Anti-Drug Center.

mains.text: India signed the Memorandum of Obligations in June 2016 and acceded to 34 SCO agreements, including the Shanghai Convention on Combating Terrorism, Separatism and Extremism.
India's chairmanship theme SECURE: Security, Economic cooperation, Connectivity, Unity, Respect for sovereignty and integrity, Environment protection, articulated at Qingdao in 2018.
After 2017 expansion SCO covered about 42% of world population, 20% of GDP and 22% of landmass.
India joined its first SCO military anti-terror drill at Chebarkul, Russia in August 2018.
India uses SCO to press zero tolerance for terrorism and greater trade, economic cooperation and connectivity.

prelims.text: CERT-In is the national agency for cyber incident response under section 70B of the IT Act 2000, appointed by notification of 27 October 2009.
CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022 under section 70B(6) require cyber incidents to be reported within 6 hours of noticing.
Directions mandate ICT logs kept for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction and clock synchronisation with NIC or NPL NTP servers.
Failure to comply with CERT-In directions may invite punitive action under section 70B(7) of the IT Act.
Data centres, VPS, cloud and VPN providers must keep accurate user registration data for five years after cancellation.
CERT-In is the national agency for responding to cyber security incidents under section 70B of the IT Act 2000.
CERT-In issued Cyber Security Directions on 28 April 2022 under section 70B(6); they became effective after 60 days.
Directions cover clock synchronisation, mandatory incident reporting, ICT log maintenance and subscriber registration by data centres, VPS, VPN and cloud providers.
Directions also set KYC norms for virtual asset service providers, exchange providers and custodian wallet providers.
National Cyber Coordination Centre, implemented by CERT-In, scans cyberspace for threats and shares metadata with agencies.
CERT-In leads CSIRT-Fin, the Computer Security Incident Response Team for the finance sector.

mains.text: Reportable incidents include ransomware, DDoS, data breaches and leaks, attacks on critical infrastructure, SCADA, digital payments, cloud systems and AI or ML systems.
Government entities must nominate a Chief Information Security Officer and report cyber incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours under its guidelines.
Reporting duty is statutory and overrides contractual confidentiality clauses under section 81 of the IT Act, CERT-In's FAQs state.
Build sectoral CSIRTs and share incident information with NIC-CERT and regulators, as CERT-In's government guidelines require.
CERT-In can call for information and issue directions to service providers, intermediaries, data centres and body corporate to coordinate incident response.
CERT-In runs an automated threat intelligence exchange platform sharing tailored alerts, and has a Cyber Crisis Management Plan for ministries, States and critical sectors.
CERT-In conducted 109 cyber security mock drills with 1,438 participating organisations and empanelled 200 security auditing organisations.
CERT-In published 44 FAQs on 18 May 2022 to clarify applicability, reporting timeframes and logging requirements of its directions.
MSMEs sought more time to comply; CERT-In extended their timeline to 25 September 2022, showing compliance burden on small entities.
Strengthen sectoral response teams such as CSIRT-Fin and regular mock drills so critical sectors can detect and contain incidents quickly.

prelims.text: Article 130: the Supreme Court sits in Delhi or other places the CJI appoints with the President's approval.
Article 136 gives the Supreme Court discretion to grant special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal, except armed forces tribunals.
Law Commission's 229th Report (5 August 2009) proposed a Constitution Bench at Delhi and four Cassation Benches at Delhi, Chennai or Hyderabad, Kolkata and Mumbai.
The Supreme Court Full Court on 18 February 2010 unanimously resolved that the Law Commission's recommendations could not be accepted.
In 2016 the Supreme Court referred the question of a National Court of Appeal to a Constitution Bench.
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice reported on 7 August 2023 recommending regional benches under Article 130.

mains.text: The Standing Committee (Chair: Sushil Kumar Modi) saw Delhi-centric access as a barrier to justice; regional benches decide appeals while constitutional matters stay in Delhi.
Law Commission's 229th Report recommended splitting the apex court into a Constitution Bench and regional Cassation Benches handling High Court appeals.
The Supreme Court has itself lamented that unfettered special leave petitions converted it into a mere court of appeal, contrary to the framers' intent for Article 136.
The Full Court found no justification for benches outside Delhi in 2010, reflecting the judiciary's resistance to restructuring.
Article 130 already lets the CJI, with the President's approval, sit outside Delhi without a constitutional amendment; the Committee said it can create four or five regional benches.
Pair any split with a case-filtering power for special leave petitions so docket pressure falls and the apex court hears fewer, constitutional matters.

prelims.text: WHO End TB Strategy 2030 targets: 80% reduction in TB incidence rate and 90% reduction in TB deaths compared with 2015.
SDG target 3.3 includes ending the TB epidemic by 2030.
RNTCP was renamed National TB Elimination Programme in 2020, aiming to eliminate TB in India by 2025.
UN held high-level meetings on TB in 2018 and 2023; 2023 funding targets are $22 billion a year by 2027 and $5 billion for research.
In 2024 India accounted for 25% of global TB cases, followed by Indonesia 10% and the Philippines 6.8%.
Catastrophic costs mean total TB costs above 20% of annual household income; the End TB target is zero such households.

mains.text: India accounts for 25% of global cases and 33% of the gap between estimated MDR/RR-TB cases and people enrolled on treatment (2024).
India accounted for 23% of global TB deaths in 2025, WHO's Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 stated.
About 50% of TB-affected households face catastrophic costs, far above the End TB target of zero.
Between 2015 and 2024 incidence fell 12% against the 50% milestone for 2025, and deaths fell 29% against 75%.
UN 2023 political declaration set coverage targets for rapid diagnostics, treatment and social benefits alongside funding and research goals for 2023-2030.
World Health Assembly in May 2026 asked WHO to develop a post-2030 global TB strategy for adoption at the 81st Assembly.

prelims.text: DPCO 2013 was notified under the National Pharmaceuticals Pricing Policy 2012 and the Essential Commodities Act 1955.
NPPA, under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, fixes ceiling prices of scheduled medicines in Schedule-I, adopted from the National List of Essential Medicines.
For non-scheduled formulations manufacturers cannot raise MRP by more than 10% over the preceding 12 months.
Paragraph 19 of DPCO 2013 gives NPPA extraordinary powers in public interest; it was first used in 2019 on 42 anti-cancer drugs.
Ceiling prices were fixed for 935 scheduled formulations as on 1 December 2025.
Consumers can check revised drug prices on the Pharma Sahi Daam app and the NPPA website.

mains.text: NPPA found non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines carry average markup of about 170%, reaching 700% or more in some cases.
The 2026 exercise covers 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs with trade margin capped at 30% of MRP, effective 9 November 2026.
The 2019 pilot on 42 drugs cut prices of about 500 brands by about 50% on average, saving about ₹984 crore annually.
Standing Committee on Chemicals and Fertilizers (6 August 2026) noted no timeframe to integrate permanent trade margin rationalisation into DPCO 2013.
Companies must maintain production and supply of notified formulations to prevent artificial shortages as margins fall.
Broaden NPPA's sales data beyond a private source covering about 70% of the market, adding hospital, Jan Aushadhi and e-commerce sales.

prelims.text: NFSA 2013 covers up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban population, which at Census 2011 is 81.35 crore persons.
Priority households get 5 kg foodgrains per person per month; Antyodaya Anna Yojana households get 35 kg per household per month.
NFSA initial subsidised prices were ₹3, ₹2 and ₹1 per kg for rice, wheat and coarse grains; the Act commenced on 5 July 2013.
PMGKAY gives free foodgrains from 1 January 2023; free distribution was extended for five years from 1 January 2024.
Section 10 of NFSA: State Governments identify Antyodaya and priority households within the coverage determined under section 9.

mains.text: ONORC lets about 81 crore beneficiaries take entitled grain from any fair price shop using ration or Aadhaar card with biometric e-PoS authentication.
ONORC particularly benefits migrant labourers and prevents duplication of ration cards.
About 80.67 crore persons were covered under NFSA against a maximum coverage of 81.35 crore.
In December 2025, 97.9% of transactions at ePOS-enabled fair price shops used Aadhaar authentication.
Duplicate or bogus ration cards still hamper targeting; ration cards are being linked with Aadhaar and a central beneficiary repository is maintained.
Extend coverage to about 79 lakh additional eligible beneficiaries and continue weeding out ineligible cards through updated lists.

prelims.text: Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme has operated since 1 April 2010 for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers.
NBS gives a fixed per-kg subsidy on nutrients N, P, K and S; rates are revised annually or biannually.
Under NBS the P&K sector is decontrolled: companies set MRP at reasonable levels, subject to government oversight.
Government makes 28 grades of P&K fertilisers available through NBS; ammonium sulphate was added from Rabi 2025-26.
Rabi 2025-26 NBS per kg of nutrient: N ₹43.02, P ₹47.96, K ₹2.38 and S ₹2.87; DAP ₹29,805 per tonne.
Boron and zinc fortified or coated P&K fertilisers receive extra subsidy of ₹300 and ₹500 per tonne respectively.

mains.text: India allocated over ₹2.04 lakh crore in NBS subsidies across 2022-23 to 2024-25 for indigenous and imported P&K fertilisers.
Tentative requirement for Rabi 2025-26 was about ₹37,952 crore, about ₹736 crore above Kharif 2025.
NBS aims to align subsidy with global price trends of fertilisers and raw materials while encouraging balanced nutrient application.
Cabinet fixes NBS rates each season considering international prices of urea, DAP, MOP and sulphur.
Because MRP is decontrolled and only monitored, farmer prices depend on government oversight of company pricing.
Encourage balanced use of N, P, K and S through nutrient-linked subsidy and fortified grades rather than reliance on urea and DAP alone.
